title: Get Ahead at Work · Episode 2
chapters: Psychological safety: why the best teams admit mistakes

units.t: Get Ahead at Work. Episode two.
In this episode: Psychological safety: why the best teams admit mistakes, Running a meeting worth attending, Speak with confidence and How to negotiate.
Part one. Psychological safety: why the best teams admit mistakes.
A researcher expected the best hospital teams to make the fewest errors.
Her data said the opposite, and that surprise changed how we think about teamwork.
A puzzling result.
In the 1990s researcher Amy Edmondson studied medication errors in hospital teams.
She expected teams with better leadership and stronger relationships to make fewer mistakes.
The data seemed to show the reverse: the better teams reported more errors.
Then she realised what might be happening.
The best teams were probably not making more mistakes.
They were more willing to talk about them, while in teams where people feared blame, errors were hidden.

That insight led to psychological safety, which Edmondson, later a Harvard Business School professor, defines as a shared belief in a team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as asking a question, admitting a mistake or raising a concern.
Google's Project Aristotle.
In 2012 Google launched Project Aristotle to find out what made some of its teams more effective than others.
Researchers studied around 180 teams, expecting the right mix of skills, personalities or backgrounds to explain success.
Those factors mattered far less than expected.
What mattered most was how team members interacted.
When Google published its findings in 2015, it listed five key dynamics: psychological safety, dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, and impact.
Psychological safety was described as by far the most important, the foundation the others depended on.
The findings drew wide attention and brought Edmondson's work to a far larger audience.
Not about being nice.
A common misunderstanding is that psychological safety means lowering expectations or avoiding criticism.
Edmondson is clear that it does not.
It also does not mean everyone agrees.
It describes the climate of a group, not one person's confidence: the same person might speak freely in one team and stay silent in another.
It means honest disagreement and bad news surface early, while there is still time to act.
She describes a grid.
Low safety and low standards produce apathy.
High safety with low standards is comfortable but unstretching.
High standards with low safety produces anxiety, and people hide problems.
The goal is high standards with high safety, her learning zone.
Candour and kindness are not opposites.
Why silence is dangerous.
The cost of silence can be enormous.
Investigations into accidents in aviation, healthcare and engineering have often found that someone saw a warning sign but hesitated to raise it with a more senior person.
From around the 1980s aviation responded with crew resource management training, which teaches junior crew to voice concerns clearly and captains to invite them.
In business the costs are usually quieter but still real: a flawed product nobody challenged, a project everyone privately doubted, a safety shortcut nobody reported.
Fear does not stop problems happening.
It mostly stops leaders hearing about them until they are much bigger and more expensive to fix.
Building it in your team.
Psychological safety can be built, and leaders have the biggest influence.
Edmondson suggests three broad practices.
First, frame the work as a learning problem rather than simple execution, being honest that there is uncertainty and that everyone's input is needed.
Second, acknowledge your own fallibility, with something as simple as saying you might be missing something.
Third, model curiosity by asking genuine questions.
Just as important is how you react when someone speaks up.
Thanking a person for raising a problem, even unwelcome news, encourages others to do the same.
Reacting with anger teaches the whole team to stay quiet.
Trust is built slowly and can be damaged very quickly.
The key idea: Amy Edmondson found that better hospital teams reported more errors, because they felt safe to speak up.
Part two. Running a meeting worth attending.
Most of us have sat through a meeting that should have been an email.
Here is how to run one people are glad they came to.
The cost of a meeting.
Picture eight people in a one hour meeting.
That is not one hour of work.
It is eight hours, nearly a full working day.
If the meeting drifts, ends without a decision and needs a follow up, the cost doubles.
Bad meetings also drain energy, interrupt focused work and teach people that their time does not matter.
Good ones can settle in thirty minutes a question that would take two weeks of emails, and get everyone moving in the same direction.
The difference is rarely luck.
Good meetings are designed, and anyone can learn how, whether you lead a team or are organising your first catch up.
Meeting or not, and who.
If you only need to share information, an email, short document or recorded update is often better.
Meetings suit things that need live conversation: decisions, tricky problems, building agreement, brainstorming and sensitive issues.
Finish this line: 'By the end of this meeting, we will have...'
If you cannot, you are not ready to book.
Put that sentence at the top of the invitation.
Invite only people who must decide, hold information you cannot get elsewhere or must carry out the outcome.
Others can read a summary.
But leaving out a key person often means redoing the meeting.
Respect different working hours, and consider twenty five or fifty minutes instead of an hour, leaving a buffer between calls.
Write a real agenda.
An agenda that says 'budget, rosters, other business' tells nobody what to prepare.
Turn each item into a question with a time: 'Which of the two venue quotes do we accept?
Ten minutes.
Read the attached comparison first.'
Put the most important item first, while energy is high, and send the agenda and any reading at least a day ahead.
Ask people to come prepared, and say so plainly.
Some teams start with a few quiet minutes to read the key document together, which levels the playing field and means nobody bluffs.
If someone wants to add an item, ask them to tell you beforehand.
An agenda is a promise about how you will use people's time.
Run the room.
Begin on time, even if someone is late, and restate the purpose in a sentence.
As chair, your job is to guide, not dominate.
Watch the clock and gently steer drifting conversations: 'Good point, let us park it.'
Keep a visible parking lot list so people know side issues have not been ignored.
Draw out quieter people by asking them directly, and politely rein in those who speak at length.
In hybrid meetings, make sure remote attendees can hear, see shared material and get a fair turn, perhaps by calling on them first.
If the discussion is going in circles, summarise where things stand and ask what is needed to decide.
End and follow up.
The last five minutes matter most, so protect them.
Read back what was decided in plain words.
List the actions: what, who and by when.
An action without a name next to it usually does not happen.
Check nobody disagrees, then finish a few minutes early.
A good test: could every attendee tell a colleague, in a sentence or two, what was decided and what they must do next?
Within a few hours, send a brief note covering decisions, actions with owners and dates, and open questions.
Store it where the team can find it.
Check on actions when due.
Review regular meetings now and then, and be willing to shorten or cancel them.
The key idea: A meeting uses everyone's time at once, so its cost is multiplied by the number of people in the room.
Part three. Speak with confidence.
The nerves never fully go away, even for professionals.
These habits make them work for you.
Nerves are normal.
Fear of public speaking ranks alongside heights and spiders in many surveys.
The racing heart, dry mouth and shaky hands are your fight-or-flight response, releasing adrenaline to prepare you for action.
Even seasoned speakers, actors and politicians feel it.
The audience notices far less than you think, an effect psychologists call the illusion of transparency.
Don't fight the feeling.
Anxiety and excitement feel alike in the body.
Harvard researcher Alison Wood Brooks found that people who said 'I am excited' aloud before a speech performed better than those who tried to calm down.
Slow breathing, with long exhales, also helps settle the body.
One big idea.
Audiences remember surprisingly little.
Decide the single message you want them to leave with, and build everything around it.
If you can't say it in one sentence, it isn't clear yet.
Cut anything that doesn't support it, however interesting.
Nobody has ever complained that a good talk finished five minutes early.

A simple structure works almost anywhere: open with a hook such as a question, a surprising fact or a short story; say what you'll cover; make two or three main points; then sum up and finish with a clear takeaway.
Stories and concrete examples stick far better than lists of facts, because our brains are wired for narrative.
Slides that help.
Slides should support what you say, not repeat it.
People can't read dense text and listen to you at the same time, so they end up doing neither well.
Use few words, large fonts, and images or simple charts that make a point at a glance.
One idea per slide is a good rule.
Never read your slides aloud.
Here is a test: if the projector died, you should still be able to give the talk.
If you couldn't, you're relying on the slides too much.
Practise out loud.
Reading your notes silently is not practice.
Rehearse the whole talk out loud, ideally standing up, at least three times.
Time it, because most people run long.
Record yourself once on your phone and watch it back.
It's uncomfortable, but you'll spot filler words like 'um', 'like' and 'you know', nervous habits like swaying, and the parts where you rush.
Know your opening lines especially well, since that's when nerves peak.
After the first minute, most people settle.
Pause, look, recover.
Nervous speakers rush.
Slow down and pause before an important point, after a question and between sections.
A pause feels endless to you but reads as confidence, gives listeners time to think and replaces filler words.
Look at real people, one at a time, for a sentence or so, rather than at the back wall or your notes.
In question time, repeat each question so everyone hears it and you gain a moment to think.
'I don't know, but I'll find out' is a fine answer.
If you lose your place, pause, glance at your notes and carry on; audiences are almost always on your side.
Every talk makes the next easier, so practise at team meetings or a Toastmasters club.
The key idea: Nerves are a natural stress response, and calling them excitement works better than trying to calm down.
Part four. How to negotiate.
Salaries, rent, car prices, bedtimes: life is full of negotiations.
A few principles reliably change the outcome.
Prepare first.
Negotiation is simply two or more sides working out an agreement.
Whether it is a pay rise, a second-hand car, a phone bill or who does the dishes, you are negotiating.
Many people avoid it because it feels awkward, and they leave money on the table.
Studies of salary offers find that people who negotiate often get more, and employers generally expect it.
Most negotiations are won before they start.
Research the market: what do similar jobs pay, what have similar cars sold for?
Decide your target, the outcome you are aiming for, and your walk-away point, the worst deal you will accept.
Anticipate the other side's concerns.
Preparation gives you confidence and stops you deciding on the spot under pressure.
Know your BATNA.
Your BATNA is your 'best alternative to a negotiated agreement': what you will do if this deal falls through.
The term comes from the 1981 book Getting to Yes by Roger Fisher and William Ury, from the Harvard Negotiation Project.
If you have another job offer, your BATNA is strong.
If you would be unemployed, it is weak.
The stronger your alternative, the more confidently you can push, and the more clearly you will know when to walk away.
Improving your BATNA, for example by getting another quote, is often the smartest move you can make.
Interests, not positions.
A position is what someone says they want.
An interest is why they want it.
The classic story: two sisters argue over one orange and finally cut it in half.
One eats the fruit and throws away the peel.
The other uses the peel for baking and throws away the fruit.
If they had asked why, both could have had all they needed.
Asking 'What's most important to you here?'
uncovers room for creative deals, like a later start date in exchange for a higher salary.
Anchor, label, wait.
The first number on the table tends to anchor the whole conversation.
If you have done your research, it often pays to make the first offer, ambitious but defensible, with a reason: 'Similar roles pay $95,000 to $105,000, and I bring X, so I'm looking for $102,000.'
If the other side anchors first with an unreasonable figure, calmly re-anchor with your own researched number.
Former FBI negotiator Chris Voss recommends 'labelling': naming the other side's feelings, like 'It sounds like budgets are tight this year.'
It shows you are listening and draws out useful information.
Ask open questions such as 'How am I supposed to do that?'
After making an offer, stop talking.
The other person will often fill the silence, sometimes with a better offer.
Trade for a fair deal.
Avoid simply splitting the difference or giving ground for nothing.
Every concession should buy something: 'I can do that price if you include delivery.'
Look beyond the headline number.
In a job negotiation there is leave, flexibility, training, title and start date.
Give ground on what is cheap for you but valuable to them, and ask for what is cheap for them but valuable to you.
If the other side feels cheated, they may not follow through or may resent you in a job you will hold for years.
Be firm on substance and friendly with people, and get the final deal in writing.
Remember your walk-away point: sometimes the best negotiation is the one where you politely say no.
The key idea: Most negotiations are won before they start, by researching the market and setting a target and walk-away point.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did the better hospital teams report more errors?
Answer. They were more willing to talk about mistakes.
Question two. Why is a one hour meeting with eight people costly?
Answer. It adds up to about eight hours of work time.
Question three. Before a nerve-racking talk, which approach did Alison Wood Brooks's research find helps performance?
Answer. Telling yourself you feel excited.
Question four. What is your walk-away point?
Answer. The worst deal you will accept.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
